name: Soft Fork
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Changing the Rules Without Splitting the Room
lesson.summary: A soft fork is a backward compatible protocol upgrade that tightens the rules for what counts as a valid block, allowing old, unupgraded nodes to keep accepting new blocks without adopting the new rules themselves.
lesson.body:
The Fork chapter described how a deliberate rule change can either keep a network unified or split it permanently in two, depending on whether old software still accepts blocks produced under the new rules. A soft fork is the version of that upgrade specifically engineered to keep old software on board. It works by only tightening the rules, making what already counted as valid a stricter subset of itself, rather than introducing something old nodes would flatly reject.

The mechanism is easier to see with a concrete shape than with an abstract description. Imagine the existing rule for a certain kind of block is simply that a value in it must be an even number. A soft fork could change that rule to say the value must be an even number that is also a multiple of four. Every block that satisfies the new, stricter rule automatically still satisfies the old rule too, since every multiple of four is also even. An old, unupgraded node checking only the original rule will still see these new blocks as valid, even though it has no idea the stricter rule exists. Only upgraded nodes are actually enforcing the tighter standard, but that is enough for the whole network to keep agreeing on one chain.

Bitcoin's Segregated Witness upgrade, activated in 2017 and usually shortened to SegWit, is a real world example of this pattern. It restructured how transaction signature data was stored and counted toward a block's size limit, which was a fairly significant change under the hood, but it was carefully designed so that old nodes, which did not understand the new signature format, would still recognize SegWit blocks as valid under the pre existing rules they already knew. Non upgraded nodes kept working and kept agreeing with upgraded ones, without ever needing to install new software themselves, exactly the outcome a soft fork is meant to produce.

This backward compatibility is a genuine engineering advantage, but it comes with a real tradeoff worth naming honestly. Old nodes that never upgrade are still validating blocks, technically, but they are no longer independently verifying the new, stricter rules the upgraded majority actually cares about, since as far as an old node can tell, nothing changed. They are effectively trusting the upgraded majority to enforce standards the old node itself cannot see or check. A soft fork therefore relies on a large enough share of the network's block producers actually adopting and enforcing the new rules for the tightened standard to mean anything in practice.

Soft forks tend to be the preferred path for changes that can be phrased as a restriction rather than an expansion, precisely because they avoid the permanent chain split that a fully incompatible change would risk. That is not a small thing for a network whose entire value depends on everyone agreeing on the same single history, and it is why protocol developers on major blockchains will often go to considerable lengths to design an upgrade as a soft fork rather than as a harder, more disruptive break from the existing rules.
